William Seward. Secretary of State under President Abraham Lincoln from 1861 to 1869, playing a crucial role in securing British and French neutrality during the Civil War while articulating a vision of American expansion. His post-war diplomacy advanced Union interests in the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific, culminating in the purchase of Alaska—an acquisition widely ridiculed but vindicated by the twentieth century.

Seward served as Lincoln's Secretary of State throughout the Civil War. His most important task was preventing European intervention, particularly from Britain and France, which might have doomed the Union. He accomplished this feat through careful diplomacy.

In 1867, he secured the Alaska Purchase, acquiring vast Alaskan territory from Russia for seven point two million dollars. The purchase was dismissed as "Seward's Folly" but has been proven strategically vital. He opposed slavery expansion into western territories, a stance that made him a Republican leader and contributed to the sectional tensions that led to war.

Seward nearly died in an assassination attempt by Confederate sympathiser Lewis Payne on the same night that Lincoln was assassinated, on April 14th, 1865. He survived and continued his work. He promoted American hegemony in the Caribbean and North Pacific through commercial treaties and strategic acquisitions. He believed the United States was destined to dominate the North American continent and extend influence across the oceans.

Abraham Lincoln was the president whom Seward served under, and their partnership was crucial to Union victory and post-war policy. Andrew Johnson succeeded Lincoln as president, and Seward retained his office and continued his vision. The American Civil War was the defining event of his tenure; his diplomacy kept Europe neutral. And his vision was rooted in the ideology of Manifest Destiny, which underpinned his expansionist foreign policy.
